body: [![CNBC](https://static-redesign.cnbcfm.com/dist/d6085c9e81f4d7365c8d.svg)](//www.cnbc.com/). [The Fed](https://www.cnbc.com/federal-reserve/). Friday's [jobs report for April](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/jobs-report-april-2026.html) provided the latest evidence that the central bank's larger concern isn't a flagging labor market but rather a [cost of living](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/consumer-sentiment-falls-to-fresh-record-low-in-may-as-surging-gas-prices-hit-outlook.html) that is getting increasingly harder for ordinary Americans to bear. At [last week's FOMC meeting](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/29/fed-interest-rate-decision-april-2026.html), three of those presidents voted against the post-meeting statement. The [consumer price index for March](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/10/cpi-inflation-report-march-2026.html) pointed to an inflation rate of 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% goal. If that's the case, though, it makes things problematic for incoming Chair [Kevin Warsh](https://www.cnbc.com/kevin-warsh/), who President Donald Trump sent to the Fed with expectations for lower rates. The former Fed governor has been open about [his preference for a lower funds rate](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/21/kevin-warsh-fed-confirmation-hearing-trump-live-updates.html), arguing that the Fed still can control inflation while easing policy. However, selling a rate cut with [inflation north of 3%](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/30/pce-inflation-rate-march-2026.html) will be a difficult job, particularly considering the leanings of the current committee structure.
